title: Compassion can be trained
hookLine: short programs at Stanford and Emory measured gains in compassion

cards: She's just a kind person. People say it the way they'd say someone is tall, or left-handed: a fixed fact. Some got the warm heart, some got the cool head, and that's the hand you're dealt.
It's a comfortable idea, especially on a day you weren't kind at all. Back on day three hundred thirteen, this path gave a short answer. Today looks closer.
Two university programs didn't ask whether some people are kinder than others. They asked: if ordinary adults practiced compassion on purpose, for a short stretch, would anything change?

teach.b: First, the programs. At Stanford, a course called Compassion Cultivation Training was developed by Thupten Jinpa, a scholar and longtime translator for the Dalai Lama.

At Emory, Cognitively-Based Compassion Training was developed by Lobsang Tenzin Negi, who teaches at Emory. Both draw on Tibetan Buddhist practice, taught in plain language, with no requirement to be Buddhist.

Second, what they practice: steadying attention, wishing yourself well, then widening the circle to someone you love, a stranger, someone difficult, and eventually everyone. Ordinary exercises, done in class and at home.
Third, what was measured. Researchers studying the Stanford course reported that people who finished it scored higher on their own reports of compassion, for others and for themselves.
Studies of the Emory program reported changes too, in measures such as reading other people's emotions from their faces.
The gains were modest, and some rest on what people say about themselves; the researchers name limits like these.
Still, something moved. Fourth, an old claim.

The Chinese philosopher Mencius, in the book that carries his name, taught that all people have a heart that can't bear to see others suffer, and that the feeling of commiseration is a beginning of goodness, like a fire that has just caught or a spring that has just begun to flow.
A beginning isn't the finished thing; Mencius said it has to be developed. Compassion isn't only a trait you have or don't. It's also a skill you can practice.

how: Secular compassion courses drawn from Tibetan Buddhist practice, such as Stanford's Compassion Cultivation Training and Emory's Cognitively-Based Compassion Training, teach people to widen a circle of goodwill from loved ones to strangers to everyone; in Confucian thought, Mencius taught that the feeling of commiseration must be developed.

games.q: what does “compassion can be trained” mean?
o: a skill that grows with practice, not a fixed trait
a rule that kindness must be forced on yourself
a claim that only monks can learn real kindness

games.q: who trained compassion: tap the pairs.
p: commiseration is a beginning to develop

s: kindness is a fixed trait you either have or don't
studies of short compassion courses reported measurable change, and Mencius called the feeling a beginning that has to be developed.
the compassion courses required people to be Buddhist
they draw on Tibetan Buddhist practice but are taught in plain language, with no requirement to be Buddhist.
the measured gains were modest, and some relied on self-report
the reported gains were modest, and some rest on what people say about themselves.

games.q: you're designing a compassion course. after wishing a loved one well, who comes next?
o: only the people you already love.
a stranger, then someone difficult, then everyone.
games.why: the courses widen the circle step by step, from easy to hard to all.

practice: Picture someone easy to love and hold one quiet wish, may you be well; then a stranger you saw this week, with the same wish; then yourself, without arguing with it.
Stay with whichever face is in mind as the time ends, and keep going afterward if you'd like the full five minutes.

wordCard.voice: Compassion can be trained. Short courses at Stanford and Emory reported modest gains, and Mencius called the feeling a beginning that has to be developed. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: trainable. Not a hand you're dealt: a beginning you can grow. Next up, kindness and bias.
